verses.note: The first word God speaks to fallen humanity is a question that seeks them out. Before judgment comes a call, and the pattern holds through Scripture to the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10).

God covers the shame they could not adequately cover themselves. Many Christian interpreters have seen in the skins the first death of an animal on humanity's behalf and a hint of sacrifice; the text does not say so, and others read the act simply as God's care for people he is sending into a harsher world. Either way the image of God clothing sinners runs through Scripture (Isaiah 61:10, Galatians 3:27).

The first mention of grace in Scripture comes at the moment of the world's condemnation. The order of verses 8 and 9, favor first and righteousness second, has long been read as showing that Noah's rescue rests on God's grace, though Genesis also insists that grace produced a righteous life.

Noah's whole household is brought in because of his standing before God. Hebrews 11:7 says Noah built the ark for the saving of his household, and the pattern of God's rescue reaching a family through one person recurs throughout Scripture.

The one who is saved does not seal his own safety; God shuts him in. The same act also marks the end of the time for entering. Jesus' parable of the ten virgins ends with the same image, the door shut when the bridegroom has come (Matthew 25:10).

This is the first remnant in Scripture: a small group preserved through judgment to carry God's purposes forward. The prophets develop the idea (Isaiah 10:20-22), and Paul applies it to the people of God saved by grace (Romans 9:27, 11:5).

Righteousness here is a right standing with God received through trust. The verse shows the way of salvation already at work in Genesis, long before the cross makes plain on what basis God can count the ungodly righteous (Romans 4:5, 23-25).

Lot is not rescued because he runs but because he is seized. The verse is one of the Old Testament's plainest pictures of salvation as God's act of mercy on the undeserving, and 2 Peter 2:7-9 draws the lesson that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly.

Lot is saved for Abraham's sake. The verse shows God's mercy reaching one person because of his covenant with another, a pattern the New Testament fulfills when believers are saved for the sake of Christ.

God's rescue here is physical survival through famine, and it is also the preservation of the line through which the promise to Abraham will come. The vocabulary of remnant and survivors will later carry the hope of rescue through judgment and exile.
